{{nowrap|[[List of Formula One World Constructors' Champions|International Cup Champion]]: [[Team Lotus|Lotus]]-[[Coventry Climax|Climax]]}} }} {{Multiple image | perrow = 3 | total_width = 450 | image1 = Jim Clark 1965.jpg | caption1 = [[Jim Clark]] won his second and final championship, driving a [[Team Lotus|Lotus]]-[[Coventry Climax|Climax]]. | image2 = Graham Hill Bestanddeelnr 924-6564.jpg | caption2 = [[Graham Hill]] finished as runner-up in the World Drivers' Championship for the third season in a row. | image3 = Jackie Stewart (1978 ABC Press photo).jpg | caption3 = [[Jackie Stewart]] finished third in his first Formula One season. | image4 = Mitter, Gerhard - Lotus1965.jpg | caption4 = [[Team Lotus|Lotus]] won the [[International Cup for F1 Manufacturers]] with the [[Lotus 25]] & [[Lotus 33|33]]. | image5 = J Crosthwaite in duffel coat with Graham Hill in BRM.jpg | caption5 = [[BRM]] finished second in the International Cup for F1 Manufacturers with the [[BRM P261]]. | image6 = BrabhamJack19650801Südkehre.jpg | caption6 = [[Brabham]] finished third in the International Cup for F1 Manufacturers with the [[Brabham BT7]] & [[Brabham BT11|BT11]]. }} The '''1965 Formula One season''' was the 19th season of [[Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile|FIA]] [[Formula One]] racing. It featured the 16th [[List of Formula One World Drivers' Champions|World Championship of Drivers]], the 8th [[List of Formula One World Constructors' Champions|International Cup for F1 Manufacturers]], and seven non-championship races open to Formula One cars. The World Championship was contested over ten races between 1 January and 24 October 1965. [[Jim Clark]] won the Drivers' Championship in a [[Team Lotus|Lotus]]-[[Coventry Climax|Climax]].{{cite web|url=https://www.formula1.com/en/results.html/1965/drivers.html|title=1965 Driver Standings|work=Formula1.com|access-date=28 March 2024}} It was his second and last championship. Lotus were also awarded the International Cup for F1 Manufacturers for the second time.{{cite web|url=https://www.formula1.com/en/results.html/1965/teams.html|title=1965 Constructor Standings|work=Formula1.com|access-date=28 March 2024}} The season saw the debut for future World Champion [[Jackie Stewart]], who finished third in the World Drivers' Championship. ==Teams and drivers== The following [[List of Formula One constructors|teams]] and [[List of Formula One drivers|drivers]] competed in the 1965 [[Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile|FIA]] [[List of Formula One World Champions|World Championship]]. {| class="wikitable sortable" style="font-size: 85%" |- ! 10 | [[Mexican Grand Prix]] | {{flagicon|MEX}} [[Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez|Magdalena Mixhuca]], [[Mexico City]] | 24 October |- |} ===Calendar changes=== * The [[South African Grand Prix]] was moved back a week, which meant it would not be the last round of [[1964 Formula One season|1964]] but the first round of 1965. * The [[French Grand Prix]] was moved from [[Rouen-Les-Essarts]] to [[Charade Circuit]] for a year. * The [[British Grand Prix]] was moved from [[Brands Hatch]] to [[Silverstone Circuit|Silverstone]], in keeping with the event-sharing arrangement between the two circuits. * The [[Dutch Grand Prix]] was moved from the middle of May to the middle of July. * The [[Austrian Grand Prix]] was run as a [[sports car racing|sports car]] race.{{cite web |title=Zeltweg 200 Miles |url=https://www.racingsportscars.com/race/Zeltweg-1965-08-22.html |website=Racing Sports Cars |access-date=28 March 2024}} ==Championship report== ===Rounds 1 to 3=== For the first time, the championship started in [[1965 South African Grand Prix|South Africa]], and it did on the very first day of the year. Sixteen drivers were invited to the event and guaranteed a place on the grid. There were four places remaining, but fourteen drivers applied. Through [[Formula One racing#Historical pre-qualifying|pre-qualifying]] and subsequent [[Formula One racing#Qualifying|qualifying]], the grid was filled. The drivers started in order of their fastest qualifying times: {{F1|1963}} champion [[Jim Clark]] in his [[Team Lotus|Lotus]]-[[Coventry Climax|Climax]] was on [[pole position]], ahead of {{F1|1964}} champion [[John Surtees]] ([[Scuderia Ferrari|Ferrari]]) and {{F1|1959}} and {{F1|1960}} champion [[Jack Brabham]] ([[Brabham]]). After the start, Clark led away with his teammate [[Mike Spence]] up to second. Not many changes in positions happened after that, until Brabham's engine started [[Engine knocking|misfiring]], leaking oil, and sending Spence in a spin on the next lap. The podium was taken by Clark, Surtees and {{F1|1962}} champion [[Graham Hill]] ([[British Racing Motors|BRM]]). Spence and Brabham finished fourth and eighth, respectively.{{cite web|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230608183404/https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/february-1965/28/11th-south-african/|url=https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/february-1965/28/11th-south-african/|title=1965 South African Grand Prix race report: Clark peerless at season opener|work=Motorsport Magazine|author=Michael Tee|date=1 January 1965|archive-date=8 June 2023|access-date=28 March 2024}} Just short of a full five months later, the [[1965 Monaco Grand Prix|Monaco Grand Prix]] was held and for this race, the organisers guaranteed one place on the grid for each factory team. The rest of the applicants had to be fast enough during qualifying to gain a starting ticket. In disagreement, Lotus decided to withdraw from the event, instead entering the [[1965 Indianapolis 500|Indianapolis 500]] a day later. Hill started on pole position, ahead of Brabham and Hill's teammate [[Jackie Stewart]]. Brabham fell back and the two BRMs led away. Hill lost a lot of time when he had to avoid a backmarker, going up the escape road and having to push his car back onto the track. On lap 30, Stewart spun coming out of the fastest corner, before Brabham's Climax engine seized. Hill made it back into the lead, ahead of the Ferraris of [[Lorenzo Bandini|Bandini]] and Surtees. [[Richard Attwood]] crashed in the hairpin, the leaders narrowly avoiding him, before [[Paul Hawkins (racing driver)|Paul Hawkins]] crashed into the harbour. His car sank to the bottom but Hawkins was unhurt, as was Attwood. Hill took the win, ahead of Bandini and Stewart, after Surtees ran out of fuel with a lap to go.{{cite web|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230716155018/https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/july-1965/32/xxiii-monaco-grand-prix/|url=https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/july-1965/32/xxiii-monaco-grand-prix/|title=1965 Monaco Grand Prix race report: Hill fights back|work=Motorsport Magazine|author=Denis Jenkinson|date=30 May 1965|archive-date=16 July 2023|access-date=28 March 2024}} For the [[1965 Belgian Grand Prix|Belgian Grand Prix]], Hill started on pole again, ahead of Clark and Stewart. Rain fell and everyone held a safe distance from the car in front, except Clark, who took the lead through the most dangerous corner on the track, the ''Masta Kink''. He quickly pulled out a big lead and even lapped Hill. Stewart finished second, ahead of [[Bruce McLaren]], Brabham and Hill. Attwood crashed at ''Masta'', his Lotus breaking in half and catching fire, but the driver escaping with only minor burns.{{cite web|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230716153511/https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/july-1965/12/belgian-grand-prix-scotland-forever/|url=https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/july-1965/12/belgian-grand-prix-scotland-forever/|title=1965 Belgian Grand Prix race report: Clark weathers the storm at Spa|work=Motorsport Magazine|author=Denis Jenkinson|date=13 June 1965|archive-date=16 July 2023|access-date=28 March 2024}} [[Jim Clark]] ([[Team Lotus|Lotus]]) was leading the Drivers' Championship with 18 points, ahead of [[Graham Hill]] ([[British Racing Motors|BRM]], 15) and debutant [[Jackie Stewart]] (BRM, 11). In the Manufacturers' Championship, BRM was leading with 19 points, ahead of Lotus (18) and [[Scuderia Ferrari|Ferrari]] (12). ===Rounds 4 to 7=== The [[1965 French Grand Prix|French Grand Prix]] was run for the first time at the [[Circuit de Charade]], which was described as a quicker, twistier version of the [[Nürburgring#Nordschleife 2|Nürburgring]].{{cite web|url=https://www.speedhunters.com/2013/08/the-volcanic-rush-of-clermont-ferrand/ |title=The Volcanic Rush of Clermont Ferrand |date=August 2013 |publisher=speedhunters.com |access-date=3 April 2017}} Championship leader [[Jim Clark]] [[Formula One racing#Qualifying|qualified]] his [[Team Lotus|Lotus]] on [[pole position]], ahead of two "number two drivers": [[Jackie Stewart]] ([[British Racing Motors|BRM]]) and [[Lorenzo Bandini]] ([[Scuderia Ferrari|Ferrari]]). Their respective team leaders, [[Graham Hill]] and [[John Surtees]], started thirteenth and fourth. Except from Bandini's accident on lap 36, the race finished as it started: Clark claimed another [[Glossary of motorsport terms#G|Grand Slam]] victory, ahead of Stewart and Surtees. Hill recovered to fifth.{{cite web|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230603050740/https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/august-1965/28/51st-grand-prix-de-iacf/|url=https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/august-1965/28/51st-grand-prix-de-iacf/|title=1965 French Grand Prix race report: A hat-trick of wins for Clark|work=Motorsport Magazine|author=Denis Jenkinson|date=27 June 1965|archive-date=3 June 2023|access-date=28 March 2024}} The [[1965 British Grand Prix|British Grand Prix]] was run at [[Silverstone Circuit|Silverstone]], where Clark scored another pole position, ahead of Hill and [[Honda F1|Honda]] driver [[Richie Ginther]]. At the start, Ginther challenged Clark for the lead, but fell back to fourth and then retired on lap 26. Surtees was fighting for third place against Lotus driver [[Mike Spence]], while his team leader suddenly slowed down. The [[Coventry Climax|Climax]] engine was losing oil and Clark was coasting round the corners, only using power on the straights. Hill did anything within his might to chase his rival down, but the Lotus hang on to finish with 3 seconds to spare. Surtees came in third.{{cite web|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230401022638/https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/august-1965/20/18th-rac-british-grand-prix|url=https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/august-1965/20/18th-rac-british-grand-prix|title=1965 British Grand Prix race report - A close thing|work=Motorsport Magazine|author=Denis Jenkinson|date=10 July 1965|archive-date=1 April 2023|access-date=28 March 2024}} [[File:Start of 1965 Dutch Grand Prix.jpg|thumb|right|The start of the [[1965 Dutch Grand Prix|Dutch Grand Prix]]]] The [[1965 Dutch Grand Prix|Dutch Grand Prix]] was run just a week later and all eyes were on Clark. It was his rival Hill, however, that scored pole position. Clark started in second, Ginther again in third. Moments before the flag fell, Lotus team owner [[Colin Chapman]] was involved in a [[punch (combat)|brawl]] with the [[Netherlands|Dutch]] [[police]]. It would result in his [[arrest]] and a two-day [[imprisonment]]. The race went on unhindered, however, and saw Ginther take the lead. On lap 5, Hill and Clark were back at the front, with the Lotus soon getting ahead. Hill then lost second place to his teammate Stewart and third place to [[Brabham]] driver [[Dan Gurney]]. Clark scored his fifth win of the season, ahead of Stewart, his fourth podium, and Gurney, his first podium of the year.{{cite web|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230605003229/https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/august-1965/13/dutch-grand-prix-4/|url=https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/august-1965/13/dutch-grand-prix-4/|title=1965 Dutch Grand Prix race report: Clark rules the dunes|work=Motorsport Magazine|author=Denis Jenkinson|date=18 July 1965|archive-date=5 June 2023|access-date=28 March 2024}} It was Clark on top again during qualifying for the [[1965 German Grand Prix|German Grand Prix]], with more than 3 seconds over the BRMs of Stewart and Hill. At the start, Surtees's gearbox went wrong and he fell back. It would lead to his retirement on lap 11. Clark and Hill were fighting for the lead, while Stewart's [[car suspension|suspension]] failed and he handed third place to Gurney. Clark broke the lap record a couple of times and won his fifth consecutive race. It was the first time since [[Jack Brabham]] in {{F1|1960}} that a driver achieved this feat. Hill was second, Gurney third.{{cite web|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220627060134/https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/september-1965/37/27th-german-grand-prix|url=https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/september-1965/37/27th-german-grand-prix/|title=1965 German Grand Prix race report: Clark king at the 'ring|work=Motorsport Magazine|author=Denis Jenkinson|date=1 August 1965|archive-date=27 June 2022|access-date=28 March 2024}} With only the top six finishes counting towards the championship, [[Jim Clark]]'s six wins crowned him the Driver's Champion with 54 points, ahead of [[Graham Hill]] ([[British Racing Motors|BRM]], 30) and [[Jackie Stewart]] (BRM, 25). Clark's six wins also gave [[Team Lotus|Lotus]] the Manufacturers' Championship, ahead of BRM (39) and [[Scuderia Ferrari]] (21). ===Rounds 8 to 10=== [[File:Jackie Stewart vainqueur de son premier Grand Prix en F1 (Monza 1965).jpg|thumb|right|[[Jackie Stewart]] won the [[1965 Italian Grand Prix|Italian Grand Prix]] in his debut season.]] Newly-crowned champion [[Jim Clark]] ([[Team Lotus|Lotus]]) achieved his fifth [[pole position]] of the year at the [[1965 Italian Grand Prix|Italian Grand Prix]], ahead of [[John Surtees]] for [[Scuderia Ferrari|Ferrari]] and [[Jackie Stewart]] for [[British Racing Motors|BRM]]. At the start, Surtees had problems with his [[clutch]], so Clark and Stewart were followed by [[Graham Hill]], who had to finish first to stay in the race for the championship. The top three were engaged in a ''slipstream battle'' and the lead changed hands lap after lap. With ten laps to go, Clark suddenly stopped with a failing [[fuel pump]], so Hill and Stewart were free to fight over the win in equal machinery. Going into the last lap, Hill touched the grass with his outer wheels, almost spinning but certainly valuable seconds. Stewart won his first race, with Hill in second and [[Dan Gurney]] in third.{{cite web|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240117073543/https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/october-1965/19/36th-italian-grand-prix/|url=https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/october-1965/19/36th-italian-grand-prix/|title=1965 Italian Grand Prix race report: Debutant's delight|work=Motorsport Magazine|author=Denis Jenkinson|date=12 September 1965|archive-date=17 January 2024|access-date=28 March 2024}} Hill started on pole for the [[1965 United States Grand Prix|United States Grand Prix]], ahead of Clark and [[Honda F1|Honda]] driver [[Richie Ginther]]. Clark quickly grabbed the lead but soon retired with a broken [[piston]]. As it had happened more often, Ginther fell back, while his [[United States|American]] rival Gurney went up the order. He came within four seconds of Hill when the [[Great Britain|Brit]] slid off the track, but when he made a mistake himself, his team leader [[Jack Brabham]] took second place. The [[Australia]]n challenged Hill for the lead, but was unable to get by, and then became the third top-runner to take to the grass. The order at the finish was Hill, Gurney, Brabham.{{cite web|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231004172637/https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/november-1965/42/grand-prix-of-the-united-states/|url=https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/november-1965/42/grand-prix-of-the-united-states/|title=1965 United States Grand Prix race report: Hill masterful at the Glen|work=Motorsport Magazine|author=Michael Tee|date=3 October 1965|archive-date=4 October 2023|access-date=28 March 2024}} The season ended with the [[1965 Mexican Grand Prix|Mexican Grand Prix]], where Clark scored another pole position, ahead of Americans Gurney and Ginther. The Honda driver took the lead at the start, while Stewart got up to second, before being passed by [[Mike Spence]]. His teammate Clark suffered his third consecutive retirement, before Stewart went out at the half-way point, and Hill's engine gave out with ten laps to go. Gurney passed Spence for second place and came within 3 seconds of the leader, but Ginther held on to his and Honda's first win.{{cite web|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230602051756/https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/december-1965/43/iv-mexican-grand-prix/|url=https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/december-1965/43/iv-mexican-grand-prix/|title=1965 Mexican Grand Prix race report: Ginther wraps it up|work=Motorsport Magazine|author=Michael Tee|date=24 October 1965|archive-date=2 June 2023|access-date=28 March 2024}} [[Jim Clark]] ([[Team Lotus|Lotus]]) was awarded the 1965 Drivers' Championship after scoring 54 points, ahead of [[Graham Hill]] ([[British Racing Motors|BRM]], 40) and [[Jackie Stewart]] (BRM, 33). The 1965 Formula One season was the 19th season of FIA Formula One racing. It featured the 16th World Championship of Drivers, the 8th International Cup for F1 Manufacturers, and seven non-championship races open to Formula One cars. The World Championship was contested over ten races between 1 January and 24 October 1965.

Jim Clark won the Drivers' Championship in a Lotus-Climax.[1] It was his second and last championship. Lotus were also awarded the International Cup for F1 Manufacturers for the second time.[2] The season saw the debut for future World Champion Jackie Stewart, who finished third in the World Drivers' Championship.

Driver changes

[edit]

Three future champions made their debuts in 1965:

  • Jackie Stewart replaced Richie Ginther at BRM, after the American driver was invited to join the Honda F1 team.
  • Denny Hulme was signed by Brabham, racing with team owner Jack Brabham and veteran Dan Gurney.
  • Having entered one race in 1964, Jochen Rindt was offered a full-time seat at Cooper, after 1961 champion Phil Hill had retired from single-seater racing.

Calendar changes

[edit]
  • The South African Grand Prix was moved back a week, which meant it would not be the last round of 1964 but the first round of 1965.
  • The French Grand Prix was moved from Rouen-Les-Essarts to Charade Circuit for a year.
  • The British Grand Prix was moved from Brands Hatch to Silverstone, in keeping with the event-sharing arrangement between the two circuits.
  • The Dutch Grand Prix was moved from the middle of May to the middle of July.
  • The Austrian Grand Prix was run as a sports car race.[3]

Championship report

[edit]

Rounds 1 to 3

[edit]

For the first time, the championship started in South Africa, and it did on the very first day of the year. Sixteen drivers were invited to the event and guaranteed a place on the grid. There were four places remaining, but fourteen drivers applied. Through pre-qualifying and subsequent qualifying, the grid was filled. The drivers started in order of their fastest qualifying times: 1963 champion Jim Clark in his Lotus-Climax was on pole position, ahead of 1964 champion John Surtees (Ferrari) and 1959 and 1960 champion Jack Brabham (Brabham). After the start, Clark led away with his teammate Mike Spence up to second. Not many changes in positions happened after that, until Brabham's engine started misfiring, leaking oil, and sending Spence in a spin on the next lap. The podium was taken by Clark, Surtees and 1962 champion Graham Hill (BRM). Spence and Brabham finished fourth and eighth, respectively.[4]

Just short of a full five months later, the Monaco Grand Prix was held and for this race, the organisers guaranteed one place on the grid for each factory team. The rest of the applicants had to be fast enough during qualifying to gain a starting ticket. In disagreement, Lotus decided to withdraw from the event, instead entering the Indianapolis 500 a day later. Hill started on pole position, ahead of Brabham and Hill's teammate Jackie Stewart. Brabham fell back and the two BRMs led away. Hill lost a lot of time when he had to avoid a backmarker, going up the escape road and having to push his car back onto the track. On lap 30, Stewart spun coming out of the fastest corner, before Brabham's Climax engine seized. Hill made it back into the lead, ahead of the Ferraris of Bandini and Surtees. Richard Attwood crashed in the hairpin, the leaders narrowly avoiding him, before Paul Hawkins crashed into the harbour. His car sank to the bottom but Hawkins was unhurt, as was Attwood. Hill took the win, ahead of Bandini and Stewart, after Surtees ran out of fuel with a lap to go.[5]

For the Belgian Grand Prix, Hill started on pole again, ahead of Clark and Stewart. Rain fell and everyone held a safe distance from the car in front, except Clark, who took the lead through the most dangerous corner on the track, the Masta Kink. He quickly pulled out a big lead and even lapped Hill. Stewart finished second, ahead of Bruce McLaren, Brabham and Hill. Attwood crashed at Masta, his Lotus breaking in half and catching fire, but the driver escaping with only minor burns.[6]

Jim Clark (Lotus) was leading the Drivers' Championship with 18 points, ahead of Graham Hill (BRM, 15) and debutant Jackie Stewart (BRM, 11). In the Manufacturers' Championship, BRM was leading with 19 points, ahead of Lotus (18) and Ferrari (12).

Rounds 4 to 7

[edit]

The French Grand Prix was run for the first time at the Circuit de Charade, which was described as a quicker, twistier version of the Nürburgring.[7] Championship leader Jim Clark qualified his Lotus on pole position, ahead of two "number two drivers": Jackie Stewart (BRM) and Lorenzo Bandini (Ferrari). Their respective team leaders, Graham Hill and John Surtees, started thirteenth and fourth. Except from Bandini's accident on lap 36, the race finished as it started: Clark claimed another Grand Slam victory, ahead of Stewart and Surtees. Hill recovered to fifth.[8]

The British Grand Prix was run at Silverstone, where Clark scored another pole position, ahead of Hill and Honda driver Richie Ginther. At the start, Ginther challenged Clark for the lead, but fell back to fourth and then retired on lap 26. Surtees was fighting for third place against Lotus driver Mike Spence, while his team leader suddenly slowed down. The Climax engine was losing oil and Clark was coasting round the corners, only using power on the straights. Hill did anything within his might to chase his rival down, but the Lotus hang on to finish with 3 seconds to spare. Surtees came in third.[9]

The Dutch Grand Prix was run just a week later and all eyes were on Clark. It was his rival Hill, however, that scored pole position. Clark started in second, Ginther again in third. Moments before the flag fell, Lotus team owner Colin Chapman was involved in a brawl with the Dutch police. It would result in his arrest and a two-day imprisonment. The race went on unhindered, however, and saw Ginther take the lead. On lap 5, Hill and Clark were back at the front, with the Lotus soon getting ahead. Hill then lost second place to his teammate Stewart and third place to Brabham driver Dan Gurney. Clark scored his fifth win of the season, ahead of Stewart, his fourth podium, and Gurney, his first podium of the year.[10]

It was Clark on top again during qualifying for the German Grand Prix, with more than 3 seconds over the BRMs of Stewart and Hill. At the start, Surtees's gearbox went wrong and he fell back. It would lead to his retirement on lap 11. Clark and Hill were fighting for the lead, while Stewart's suspension failed and he handed third place to Gurney. Clark broke the lap record a couple of times and won his fifth consecutive race. It was the first time since Jack Brabham in 1960 that a driver achieved this feat. Hill was second, Gurney third.[11]

With only the top six finishes counting towards the championship, Jim Clark's six wins crowned him the Driver's Champion with 54 points, ahead of Graham Hill (BRM, 30) and Jackie Stewart (BRM, 25). Clark's six wins also gave Lotus the Manufacturers' Championship, ahead of BRM (39) and Scuderia Ferrari (21).[11]

Rounds 8 to 10

[edit]

Newly-crowned champion Jim Clark (Lotus) achieved his fifth pole position of the year at the Italian Grand Prix, ahead of John Surtees for Ferrari and Jackie Stewart for BRM. At the start, Surtees had problems with his clutch, so Clark and Stewart were followed by Graham Hill, who had to finish first to stay in the race for the championship. The top three were engaged in a slipstream battle and the lead changed hands lap after lap. With ten laps to go, Clark suddenly stopped with a failing fuel pump, so Hill and Stewart were free to fight over the win in equal machinery. Going into the last lap, Hill touched the grass with his outer wheels, almost spinning but certainly valuable seconds. Stewart won his first race, with Hill in second and Dan Gurney in third.[12]

Hill started on pole for the United States Grand Prix, ahead of Clark and Honda driver Richie Ginther. Clark quickly grabbed the lead but soon retired with a broken piston. As it had happened more often, Ginther fell back, while his American rival Gurney went up the order. He came within four seconds of Hill when the Brit slid off the track, but when he made a mistake himself, his team leader Jack Brabham took second place. The Australian challenged Hill for the lead, but was unable to get by, and then became the third top-runner to take to the grass. The order at the finish was Hill, Gurney, Brabham.[13]

The season ended with the Mexican Grand Prix, where Clark scored another pole position, ahead of Americans Gurney and Ginther. The Honda driver took the lead at the start, while Stewart got up to second, before being passed by Mike Spence. His teammate Clark suffered his third consecutive retirement, before Stewart went out at the half-way point, and Hill's engine gave out with ten laps to go. Gurney passed Spence for second place and came within 3 seconds of the leader, but Ginther held on to his and Honda's first win.[14]

Jim Clark (Lotus) was awarded the 1965 Drivers' Championship after scoring 54 points, ahead of Graham Hill (BRM, 40) and Jackie Stewart (BRM, 33). Lotus clinched the Manufacturers' Championship as well, with 54 points, ahead of BRM (45), with Brabham just overtaking Ferrari for third place (27 and 26 points, respectively).
